name: Ink to Internet: How Information Learned to Travel
description: Clay, paper, type, wires, waves and packets: the machines that let ideas cross the world faster each century, and the people who built them.

checkpoints.name: Pen and block
checkpoints.note: Egyptians wrote on papyrus, Cai Lun in China helped perfect paper, and printers there carved blocks of wood and later set movable type, ideas that spread slowly along trade routes.

checkpoints.name: The press
checkpoints.note: Gutenberg's press in Germany made books cheap and quick to copy. Pamphlets, newspapers and learned letters multiplied, and reading became part of ordinary life.

checkpoints.name: Wires and waves
checkpoints.note: The telegraph, Morse code, the telephone and the penny post sped messages up to the pace of the wire, and a cable under the Atlantic joined two continents in 1858. Marconi's wireless radio reached ships and homes, and television followed in the 1920s and 1930s.

checkpoints.name: Packets and satellites
checkpoints.note: Satellites such as Sputnik and Telstar beamed signals across the sky and optical fibre began to carry light signals. Researchers invented packet switching, built ARPANET and sent the first email, and Kahn and Cerf devised the protocol that lets networks join together.

checkpoints.name: The web era
checkpoints.note: Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web and the Mosaic browser opened the internet to everyone. Search, Wikipedia, social networks and the iPhone then put it in every pocket.
